title: The Frank Johnson band as an ensemble
summary: The Johnson band had no single star; its strength was ensemble playing, and joining it improved Polites at once. Clarinettist Jeff Kitchen and trombonist Warwick Dyer are mentioned.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: Well, uh, back to Frank Johnson. Who was the star of that band? Was Johnson himself a star? I know.

Was it a star? Um, no, it was, uh, it was a, uh, a good all-round band. That was the, uh, basis of it. And, uh, it was a great band to play with. Um. I remember the first time I, I played with them, uh, I became, uh, 50% better player straight away because, uh, everyone played so well, it was so easy to fit in with them. Um. They, uh, when they started, their star was, uh, just a big star. And then, uh, there was, uh, Jeff Kitchen, a clarinet player. Mm-hm. And after he left, um, Warwick Dyer, the trombone player, grew in statue, and, uh, very nice player. Unfortunately killed in an automobile accident. Um, but, uh, the Frank Johnson band was, uh, its, uh, strength was that it was, uh, playing as a band, and, uh, its ensemble work was its forte. Mm-hm. I see.
